source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Core claim: reward is treated as just another observation. The agent has a prior preference over that observation. Flatten the preference and reward has no effect on the value function.
numbers: Paper compares 5 agents on a 3x3 FrozenLake variant: Q-learning (eps 0.1), Q-learning (eps decaying 1 to 0), Bayesian model-based RL (Thompson sampling), active inference, and a null active inference agent with no preferences.
quote: reward is -- by definition -- some outcome that reinforces behavior, and hence a circular definition
limits: This is a conceptual and simulation paper, not a human study. The authors say the equivalence is not exact: changing the environment is not the same as changing the agent.
agent_relevance: Open mode: our agent can treat a goal as a preference over outcomes, and drop the preference to get pure exploration.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Setup details. FrozenLake 3x3, start at position 1, goal (G) and hole (H) at positions 6 and 8 or the reverse. Episode ends at G or H. Max 15 moves. Q-learning: learning rate 0.5, discount 0.99. Bayesian RL: Dyna-style, Beta pseudo-counts start at 1, k=50 sampled MDPs solved by value iteration, discount 0.9.
numbers: 200 trials x 500 episodes per agent. Non-stationary variant swaps G and H at episodes 21, 121, 141, 251, 451.
limits: Tiny state space. Authors admit the Bayesian RL agent is naive and a richer one (explicit context beliefs) might match active inference.
agent_relevance: Shows how weak the RL baselines are. Do not read the win as a general result.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Table 1, deterministic world: all reward-seeking agents solve it. Active inference scores 99.88, Bayesian RL 99.76, Q-learning eps 0.1 97.79, Q-learning decaying 80.44, null active inference 50.03.
numbers: Average reward over 200 trials x 500 episodes. 95% CI: active inference [99.64, 100.00]; Bayesian RL [99.45, 100.00]; Q-learning decaying [78.96, 81.93]; null [49.70, 50.35].
limits: Table text was extracted from PDF with some column scrambling; row mapping read from layout and consistent with the text (all agents above 80 except null).
agent_relevance: In a stable world, an explicit preference is enough. The null agent at 50 shows what no goal gives: a coin flip between goal and hole.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Table 1, stochastic/non-stationary world: active inference stays at 98.90. Both Q-learning agents and Bayesian RL fall to about 64 to 66.
numbers: Active inference 98.90 [98.00, 99.79]; Q-learning eps 0.1 66.08 [63.28, 68.88]; Q-learning decaying 65.13 [62.57, 67.68]; Bayesian RL 64.39 [60.33, 68.44]; null 50.22.
limits: Same toy task. The RL agents had no context-switch machinery. The paper itself notes this.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping an explicit context or hypothesis variable that can flip, instead of slowly accumulated counts.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: After a goal swap, RL agents lost performance for about 40 episodes. Active inference recovered after one episode because its model infers that a switch happened.
numbers: Performance of all goal-seeking agents dropped to 0 at episode 21. Q-learning and Bayesian RL needed about 40 episodes. Bayesian RL got slower at each later swap because pseudo-counts piled up. Q-learning eps 0.1 adapted faster than Bayesian RL.
limits: Only 5 swaps. The result depends on the generative model already encoding two possible goal locations.
agent_relevance: Pre-listing the possible worlds (hypotheses) lets the agent switch in one step. This fits an explicit hypothesis set in the scaffold.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Reward shaping test (Table 2). With any positive goal reward, Bayesian RL and active inference behave almost the same. Q-learning is more sensitive to living costs.
numbers: With goal reward 100: Q-learning 95.3 to 96.5 score, 3.4 to 3.6 moves; Bayesian RL 99.7 to 99.9, 3.0 moves; active inference 99.5 to 99.6, 3.0 to 3.07 moves. Reward -100 maps to preference -log(5). 100 agents x 100 episodes.
limits: Q-learning there was evaluated on-policy (eps 0). Only FrozenLake.
agent_relevance: Rewards and preferences are interchangeable when you convert reward into log-probability. A prompt-level goal can be encoded either way.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Reward-free case, first row of Table 2: Q-learning learns nothing and loops. The belief-based agents keep exploring.
numbers: No reward at all: Q-learning score 0.00 with 15 moves (circular policy, hits the time limit). Bayesian RL 39.94 (9.17 moves). Active inference 44.00 (8.67 moves). Authors describe scores of 40 to 45 as ongoing exploration.
limits: Exploration in the Bayesian RL agent comes from uncertainty over its model, not from a reward. Scores of 40 to 45 are just goal or hole hits at random.
agent_relevance: Open mode: a belief-based agent keeps acting without reward; a pure reward learner stalls. Our agent should hold uncertainty over its own model.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Negative-only preference: all three approaches avoid the hole but never seek the goal, so they run to the time limit.
numbers: Row 2 of Table 2: score 0.00 and 15 moves for Q-learning, Bayesian RL and active inference. Belief agents avoid both positions 6 and 8 since they do not know which is the hole.
limits: Illustrates that a bare avoid-signal gives no direction.
agent_relevance: Warns that negative-only constraints (guardrails) do not give goal-seeking. Pair constraints with a positive aim.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Reward-free learning of the world model gives purposeful exploration: the agent covers unvisited states and does not revisit.
numbers: Likelihood-only learning (Dirichlet counts start at 5), simulated 15 times; first episode trajectory is right, right, down, right (6 to 6), no revisits. Behaviour persists across later episodes with new non-overlapping trajectories.
limits: Shown as trajectory figures (Figure 5), not as a statistical comparison with an RL curiosity method such as RND or ICM.
agent_relevance: Open mode exploration without reward is possible when the agent scores actions by expected information gain.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Learning preferences from experience can lock in odd goals. If the hole is hit first, the agent learns to prefer holes. If Frisbee is hit first, it prefers Frisbee. After about 5 episodes with both learned, it goes straight to the hole and stops exploring.
numbers: Preference Dirichlet prior starts at 1. 10 simulations per case; with both likelihood and preferences learned, 10 simulations, hole-seeking after 5 trials.
quote: I am the sort of creature that enjoys spending time in holes
limits: Self-reinforcing preference is a failure mode for reward design. The paper presents it as a feature (self-evidencing).
agent_relevance: Risk for an open-mode agent: whatever it does first can become what it wants. Need a check against drift in what it prefers.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: Free energy of the expected future (FEEF) objective: reward is a separate observation with a preferred distribution, plus information gain over states and parameters. Implemented as model-based planning with CEM and an ensemble.
numbers: Tasks: Mountain Car and Cup Catch (sparse), Half Cheetah run and flip (shaped), Ant Maze (no reward). 5 seeds. Mountain Car: 25 episodes, up to 200 steps each.
limits: Workshop paper, 5 seeds, no formal statistics. FEEF differs from the original expected free energy; the paper says so.
agent_relevance: Information-gain bonus plus preference target in one score is a design pattern for a planning step.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: Sparse reward: FEEF reached the Mountain Car goal and hit optimal performance in a single trial. Reward-only and variance-seeking baselines mostly failed. On Cup Catch all agents did about the same by roughly 20 episodes.
numbers: Mountain Car: optimal return after trial 1 for FEEF; baselines (reward-only; variance + extrinsic) on average unable to reach the goal. Cup Catch: all asymptote around 20 episodes.
limits: Cup Catch goal can be hit by random action, so directed exploration helped little. Eyeballed from plots.
agent_relevance: Directed exploration pays off when reward is hard to find by luck, and not otherwise.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: Shaped reward and no reward. On Half Cheetah the model-based FEEF agent beat SAC after 100 episodes. In reward-free Ant Maze it covered much more of the maze than a random agent.
numbers: Half Cheetah run and flip: FEEF above SAC level after 100 episodes, 5 seeds. Ant Maze coverage (percent of maze): FEEF clearly above random baseline (exact percentages only in figure, not in text).
limits: Baseline in Ant Maze is random actions, a weak comparison. SAC reference number is one point, not a learning curve.
agent_relevance: Reward-free exploration beats random walk; but the bar is low.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: Formal link: FEEF is an upper bound on the KL between expected and preferred observations used in control-as-inference. So active inference sits next to probabilistic RL, not apart.
numbers: Appendix D bound: FEEF >= KL[p(o|pi) || p(o)].
limits: Bound is on one formulation. Paper footnote says FEEF is not the standard expected free energy.
agent_relevance: Goal-matching as divergence from a desired outcome distribution.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2022) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Proof: standard discrete active inference gives Bellman-optimal actions only for planning horizon 1. Sophisticated inference (recursive) matches backward induction on any finite horizon.
numbers: Theorem 15 (horizon T=1, zero temperature, known MDP) and Theorem 16 (backward induction as active inference). Standard scheme sums weighted expected free energy over whole future paths, so it differs from backward induction beyond one step.
limits: Applies to finite-horizon MDPs with known transitions and a Dirac-style preference over reward-maximising trajectories. POMDP extension needs extra assumptions. Not a learning-speed result.
agent_relevance: Reward maximisation is a special case of active inference. For multi-step plans, evaluate step by step recursively, not by summing whole-path scores.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2022) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Review of the exploration claim and of human data: humans are not pure reward maximisers, they use random and directed exploration. Active inference gives directed exploration through epistemic value, and random exploration by sampling from the action posterior.
numbers: Cites Daw 2006, Wilson 2014, Mirza 2018, Schulz and Gershman 2019 for human exploration. Says explore-then-exploit beats the converse.
quote: active inference agents will explore until enough uncertainty is resolved for reward maximising, goal-seeking imperatives to start to predominate
limits: Argument from literature, no new data in this paper. Authors say it is open which objective humans actually optimise.
agent_relevance: Supports two exploration modes in open mode: directed (information gain) and sampled (temperature).

source: Fountas, Sajid, Mediano, Friston (2020) Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods
finding: Deep active inference with Monte Carlo tree search planning (DAIMC), tested on a dSprites sorting task and Animal-AI. Trained agents explore first, then switch to reward-seeking once the model is confident.
numbers: Compared 3 expected free energy forms (states only; states plus parameters; down-weighted reward) vs a reward-maximising baseline. All collected similar reward; active inference agents visited more positions per round and reconstructed expected reward better.
limits: Authors say the comparison is illustrative, not a thorough benchmark.
agent_relevance: Explore then exploit emerges from one objective. A scaffold can mimic it with an uncertainty-dependent switch.

source: Fountas, Sajid, Mediano, Friston (2020) Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods
finding: On Animal-AI, DAIMC with 2M learning iterations beat DQN and A2C and was comparable to PPO2, with lower variance across runs than PPO2.
numbers: Baselines from OpenAI baselines with default settings; best DAIMC at 16 MCTS loops and decision threshold 0.1 (Animal-AI); dSprites best at threshold about 0.8. Full DAIMC training took about 4 days on dSprites with the MCTS planner.
limits: Default hyperparameters for the baselines. Single environment. Compute cost of MCTS is high.
agent_relevance: Planning cost and a decision threshold (stop searching when one option dominates) matter.

source: Sajid, Tigas, Zakharov, Fountas, Friston (2021) Exploration and preference satisfaction trade-off in reward-free learning
finding: Pepper: model-based Bayesian agent that learns preferences with no reward, using conjugate (Dirichlet) priors added to expected free energy. Tested in FrozenLake and a 3D TileWorld with volatility.
numbers: FrozenLake: original reward 10 for goal and -0.25 for hole, removed here, a sub-goal tile added. Volatility = map change every K steps: 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 percent (K = none, 40, 20, 10, 1). 10 seeds.
limits: Authors state reward-free removes the designer's only control channel; not suitable where behaviour must be controlled.
agent_relevance: Preference learning gives an adaptive agent but one you cannot steer. Keep a human-set anchor.

source: Sajid, Tigas, Zakharov, Fountas, Friston (2021) Exploration and preference satisfaction trade-off in reward-free learning
finding: Inverted U between environment volatility and preference satisfaction. Exploration peaks at 50 percent volatility (highest Hausdorff distance), then falls back at 100 percent.
numbers: State preference learning: highest Hausdorff distance (most varied trajectories) at 50 percent volatility. At 100 percent the agents learn bimodal preferences and go straight to a target regardless of map (noisy-TV like).
limits: 10 seeds; effect read from a figure. Reward preference learning showed no clear difference since neutral tiles dominated counts. Cannot generalise beyond these grids.
agent_relevance: Fully random noise can be ignored by a preference-learning agent. This is the noisy-TV problem handled without a special trick.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Seth, Buckley (2020) On the relationship between active inference and control as inference
finding: Formal comparison of active inference and control-as-inference: control-as-inference adds exogenous optimality variables and keeps the world model clean. Active inference builds value into the world model as biased priors.
numbers: Different functionals: control-as-inference has an observation-ambiguity term that active inference lacks; active inference has expected information gain that control-as-inference lacks.
quote: AIF approaches thus lend themselves naturally to goal-directed exploration whereas CAI mandates only random, entropy-maximizing exploration.
limits: Theory only, no experiments.
agent_relevance: Keep the factual model and the goal model separate where possible (cleaner), but know that goal-biased beliefs are what give directed exploration.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: The expected free energy is not simply the free energy of the future. A more natural extension discourages exploration. Information gain only appears because of how EFE is defined.
numbers: Shows EFE = free energy of the future minus expected information gain. Proposes FEEF as a compromise that keeps the information-seeking term.
limits: Pure theory. This is a critique of the standard derivation, not of the behaviour.
agent_relevance: Epistemic drive is a design choice that is added, not a free consequence. Our scaffold should add it on purpose.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2019) Scaling active inference
finding: Early scaled implementation: active inference with learned model on continuous control. About an order of magnitude better sample efficiency than DDPG on inverted pendulum and hopper.
numbers: Converged in under 100 epochs, DDPG compared over 1500 epochs. 5 seeds. Only the extrinsic term was used here because rewards were shaped.
limits: Only extrinsic value in the exploitation test, so not a test of the epistemic part. Gain is likely from being model-based.
agent_relevance: The sample-efficiency gain is a model-based effect, not special to active inference.

source: Hafner, Ortega, Ba, Parr, Friston, Heess (2022) Action and perception as divergence minimization
finding: Action Perception Divergence: places task reward, information gain, empowerment and skill discovery on one spectrum of divergence objectives. Compares itself with active inference.
numbers: Argues active inference maximises probability of inputs under the model, which gives smaller niches in noisy worlds, and optimises exploration terms only through actions.
limits: Framework paper with a taxonomy. Read the abstract, comparison section and references; not all appendices.
agent_relevance: Task rewards are optional once an agent has a good world model and an information drive.

source: Wen (2025) The Missing Reward: Active Inference in the Era of Experience
finding: Position paper: replace external rewards with free energy minimisation, and use an LLM as the world model inside an active inference loop (named the grounded-agency gap).
numbers: Conceptual only. The author says the LLM-AIF architecture is high level and lists open questions: EFE computation, and the interface between LLM representations and belief updates.
limits: No experiment, no measured result. Do not count as evidence of benefit.
agent_relevance: Shows interest in the idea. Gives no test of it.

source: Prakki (2024/2025) Active inference for self-organizing multi-LLM systems
finding: Active inference layer above an LLM research agent, picking prompts and search actions. Model has 3 state factors (prompt, search, information) and 7 observation modalities.
numbers: Result is qualitative: observation matrices move away from uniform, and action selection shifts from search toward prompt testing. No comparison to an RL baseline or a random baseline is reported in the text I read.
limits: Fixed state space of predefined prompts. LLM scores the search results, so the observations are LLM-judged. Author lists dynamic state space and hierarchy as future work.
agent_relevance: Closest actual LLM use found: a discrete active inference controller around an LLM. Evidence of benefit is thin.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020/2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Authors list limits: only FrozenLake, a naive RL baseline, and behavioural equivalence only holds in this set-up. A maze with a noisy attractor and no reward might show differences.
numbers: Said directly in the text: stronger RL such as context-belief agents should be compared.
limits: This is the key boundary condition of the founding study. No independent replication of the FrozenLake table was found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Treat the 98.9 vs 64 gap as an existence demo.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2022) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Second-hand: Cullen et al. (2018) reported active inference agents did better than reward-maximising agents in the Doom gym task, but those reward-maximisers were active inference agents without the epistemic term, not standard RL.
numbers: Sajid et al. state this in section 3; Cullen paper itself not opened.
limits: Second-hand. Source paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Weak support: epistemic term helps in a reward task.
